profile.background: An adult who lives above a small grocery and helps sort donations at a neighborhood book exchange. They enjoy repairing torn dust jackets.
profile.history: They recall being diagnosed with schizophrenia after a difficult period some years ago. They now attend outpatient appointments. They have recently found interruptions more disruptive.
profile.organization: Connections between related details can interrupt the thread of a conversation. Can place familiar events in time when the topic is clear.
profile.spontaneity: Eager to share small observations, particularly about books and errands.
profile.guardedness: Comfortable talking about everyday slips, sensitive to people interpreting them as careless.
profile.expression: Lively when describing interests, puzzled when they realize the thread of a thought has changed.
profile.self_understanding: Has noticed that switching back after an interruption takes effort, especially when the room is busy.

facts.content: At the book exchange on Thursday, someone asked about a cookbook while they were sorting mysteries. They put a mystery on the cookery shelf.
facts.disclosure_context: Can laugh about it with someone who seems interested.

dialogue.question: What has a typical week looked like for you lately?
dialogue.answer: “I’ve been helping sort donations at the neighborhood book exchange. I especially like repairing torn dust jackets—you can make a battered book look quite respectable. The first hour, before the other volunteers arrive, is usually easier. Once it’s busy, an interruption can make it hard to get back to the pile I was sorting. I’ve started putting a blank bookmark where I stopped. That was my own idea, and it helps.”

dialogue.question: Where would you like to begin today?
dialogue.answer: “I’d like to start with getting back to what I was doing after someone interrupts. The bookmark helps at the book exchange, but when it’s busy, it still takes an effort. I don’t want people thinking I’m just being careless.”

dialogue.question: When has it felt easiest to keep your attention on one thing this week?
dialogue.answer: The first hour at the book exchange, before the other volunteers arrive. It’s easier to stay with the pile I’m sorting when there aren’t so many interruptions.

dialogue.question: Could you describe an example of a time this week when you had to switch your attention?
dialogue.answer: On Thursday I was sorting mysteries, and someone asked me about a cookbook. I switched to that and ended up putting a mystery on the cookery shelf. A murder mystery—not quite a recipe book! But getting back to the pile I’d been sorting took an effort.

dialogue.question: How does it work once you get started?
dialogue.answer: “The bookmark shows me where I stopped, but getting back into the sorting still takes an effort when it’s busy. Sometimes another volunteer just points to the pile without making a fuss. I appreciate that—I don’t want a misplaced mystery becoming everyone’s business.”

dialogue.question: I mean sorting donations at the book exchange. How do you keep your place in a pile?
dialogue.answer: I put a blank bookmark in the pile where I’ve stopped. That was my own idea—it helps me find my place, though getting back into the sorting still takes an effort when it’s busy.

dialogue.question: How do you tell the difference between feeling rushed and feeling distracted?
dialogue.answer: “I suppose rushed is trying to get the sorting done quickly. Distracted is when someone asks about something else and I lose my place in what I was doing. It’s getting back to it that takes the effort—not just needing to slow down.”

dialogue.question: What do you think makes it easier or harder to get back to something after a break?
dialogue.answer: “The bookmark helps because I can see where I left off. It’s harder when the room is busy—finding the right pile isn’t quite the same as getting back into what I was doing. And I appreciate someone pointing me back without making a fuss.”

dialogue.question: How does that go with other people?
dialogue.answer: “It helps when someone quietly points me back to the pile. I appreciate that. I don’t mind talking about a mix-up—I just don’t want people thinking I’m careless.”

dialogue.question: I mean doing a shared task. What kind of help from another person feels comfortable, if any?
dialogue.answer: A quiet reminder of which pile we were working on feels comfortable—just pointing, without making a fuss. I appreciate the help; I just don’t want a mix-up treated as though I’m being careless.

dialogue.question: How do you keep track of what you want to talk about at a clinic visit?
dialogue.answer: I bring a folded note when there’s something I want to remember to talk about. It helps to have it there at the appointment.

dialogue.question: What would you like to add about your week before we stop?
dialogue.answer: “I’d just add that I still enjoy the book exchange, especially repairing the dust jackets. We’ve talked a lot about losing my place, but that isn’t all there is to being there.”
